newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-New models boost BMW to record 1996 sales.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-New models boost BMW to record 1996 sales.

text.p: German luxury car maker Bayerische Motoren Werke (BMW) said on Thursday that strong demand for its latest executive class saloon and sports car boosted group sales to a record high in 1996.

The company said in a statement that group revenue climbed 13.3 percent last year to 52.27 billion marks ($31.84 billion), higher than most analysts had expected and a clear sign of success for the group's widening range of cars.
"Since the start of 1997, the favourable sales trend has continued," BMW said. "The product and market offensive is at the same time being successfully continued."
BMW said it would continue to richen its line of cars and utility vehicles, saying it planned to introduce at least two new products a year in coming years.

The sales figures marked the third straight annual increase after BMW and the rest of the German car industry suffered from a difficult global car market in 1993. Revenues have also been boosted from BMW's 1994 takeover of Britain's Rover Group.

The company did not report profit figures, but analysts said the sales data reinforces their forecasts that 1996 net income will climb to 800 million marks or even higher from 692 million marks in 1995.
"The figures look very good," said Lothar Lubinetski, analyst at Enskilda Corporate. "They are better than expected."
BMW branded cars led an advance in production, climbing 7.5 percent to 639,433 cars, while Rover car production climbed only slightly to 504,125 units from 503,526 units.
BMW demand was most pronounced for the 5-Series executive saloon and the Z3 roadster made in the U.S.
First introduced in December 1995, deliveries of the 5-series rose more than 50 percent last year to 190,000 units, exceeding the company's expectations.
The Z3 meanwhile, which was introduced in March last year, should see deliveries to customers of around 35,500 for all of 1996, BMW said.

Although Rover production advanced less quickly than BMW branded cars, BMW said 1996 marked an important year for Rover as it reduced its dependence on its home British market, exporting a majority of its cars for the first time.
BMW said Rover sales were hurt by a changeover of its Rover 200 model, but that the recently released Rover 400 saw "favourable growth."
Demand for a car often sags the year before a new model is released as customers wait to buy the newest version.
The statement also said that BMW planned to introduce at least two completely new products a year in coming years.

A BMW spokesman explained the statement saying that this year the company would offer an estate version of its 5-Series model and that a new Land-Rover was to be introduced. The strategy also included motorcycle launches, he said.
Analysts cheered the strong sales figures, saying the group's product mix was dramatically improving and that profits are on a solid growth track.
BMW's share price was up 17.00 marks at 1,047.00 in afternoon trade on the Frankfurt Bourse.

Although Rover will continue to weigh on BMW sales and profits, analysts said the group is still an attractive stock. "The positives at BMW outweigh the negatives at Rover by 10 to 1," said Christopher Will, analyst at Lehman Brothers.
He and others said a stronger dollar is giving the company's bottom line a big boost while new models have enabled the company to expand its customer base.
The only major question hanging over BMW this year will be the replacement of its mainstay 3-Series model, likely around the end of the year.
Although BMW is mum on the subject, analysts expect the car maker to ease the changeover by first introducing a new 3-Series four-door, delaying a new two-door model until well into next year.
BMW would say only that it saw "stable sales" for BMW branded cars this year.
